summary: Describes the background behind removing the on-link assumption from IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. Under the original algorithm, a host with no default router assumed all destinations were on-link, which caused problems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If you do not know where the road leads, guessing that everyone is next door is risky. This explains why that guess was removed.

questions: what is the ipv6 on-link assumption
why was the on-link assumption removed
what happens when ipv6 has no default router
subtitle: Why IPv6 Neighbor Discovery stopped assuming every destination is on the local link when no router is known.

tldr.problem: The original Neighbor Discovery sending algorithm said a host with an empty default router list should assume all destinations are on-link, which caused delays, ambiguity and security problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the background and the harm, and records the text that was removed from the Neighbor Discovery specification: with no route, a destination is unreachable and the node reports ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable instead of attempting address resolution.
tldr.outcome: The assumption was removed in RFC 4861, and the removal addresses the security issues the RFC describes.

today: RFC 4943 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The change it documents lives in RFC 4861, which removed the on-link assumption from Neighbor Discovery.

sections.title: The On-Link Assumption
sections.content:
In RFC 2461, the host sending algorithm said that if the default router list is empty, the sender assumes the destination is on-link. It was meant to let two systems with different global prefixes talk over one link with no router, for example when plugged in back to back.

RFC 4943 argues that the problems this assumption causes outweigh that benefit, and that the back-to-back case should be treated as a misconfiguration. Systems should instead share a common prefix such as the link-local prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said that if you have no map, assume everybody lives on your street. It helps when two friends meet on one street, but it misleads in many other cases.

sections.title: The Problems It Caused
sections.content:
Hosts with IPv6 enabled but no off-link IPv6 connectivity resolve names to AAAA and A records and may try unreachable IPv6 destinations. The RFC lists these problems:

  • Address selection: the first rule of RFC 3484 destination selection is "Avoid unusable destinations", but the assumption can make an unreachable IPv6 destination look reachable and be preferred over a reachable IPv4 one.
  • Delays: link-layer address resolution must be tried for every address, taking no less than 3 seconds, and TCP may retransmit for at least 3 minutes before aborting.
  • Multiple interfaces: with several links it is unclear which link to use. Sending on one link may pick the wrong one, sending on all is complex and ambiguous, and dropping is the same as not making the assumption.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine knocking on every door on the street to find a friend who lives in another city. You waste lots of time before trying the right place.

sections.title: Security Problems
sections.content:
The assumption weakens security in two ways. Attackers can "kill" a host's default router, causing it to send everything on-link where the attacker can spoof off-link nodes; this is the "Default router is killed" threat in RFC 3756.

Second, some VPN software that does not support IPv6 sends IPv6 packets in the clear to the local media. A malicious third party could then spoof the destination on-link. The RFC states that removing the assumption addresses all the security issues it describes.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bully can make you lose your guide, you start trusting anyone nearby. Without the guess, you simply do not send the message until you know the route.

sections.title: What Changed in Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Between RFC 2461 and RFC 4861, three edits were made. The sentence "If the Default Router List is empty, the sender assumes that the destination is on-link" was removed from Section 5.2. Bullet item 3 in Section 6.3.6, which said to assume all destinations are on-link if the list is empty, was removed. Appendix A was changed to drop related text about multihomed hosts missing Router Advertisements.

The result is that a destination with no routing information is unreachable. Instead of attempting link-layer address resolution, a node should send an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable message (code 0, no route to destination) up the stack.
sections.plainLanguage: Now the rule is: no route, no guessing. The computer just says that it does not know how to get there.
